opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, because the honest answer is that we try to hold a few different time horizons in our heads at once.

On the practical side, a lot of our work is focused on the next few years. We ask what the systems we're likely to train in the near term could actually do, and what could go wrong if they're more capable than we expect. That covers things like dangerous capability evaluations, monitoring, and making sure our mitigations are ready before the capabilities arrive rather than after. We don't want to be in a position where a model crosses some threshold and we're only then starting to figure out what to do about it.

But we also try to think further out, toward systems that are genuinely more capable than humans across a wide range of domains. Our current techniques might stop working at that point. If your oversight depends on a human being able to check the model's work, what happens when the model is better than the human at the task? That's why we invest in things like amplified oversight, debate, and interpretability. The bet there is that these could keep scaling even once we can't directly verify everything ourselves.

One framing I find useful is to treat our plans as an "anytime" approach. We want something reasonable to do if powerful AI shows up surprisingly soon, even if it's not the ideal solution. Then, if we have more time, we can build toward more robust and principled approaches. There's a lot of uncertainty about timelines, so planning only for the long term or only for the short term seems like a mistake.

I'd also say there's a limit to how far ahead you can usefully plan in detail. The field changes quickly, and the specifics of what future systems look like really matter for what safety work makes sense. So we keep a rough picture of the long-term problem, especially misalignment and misuse, and then try to update our concrete plans fairly often as we learn more.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the guest, with no tools.

That's a good question, and I'd say the honest answer is that it varies a lot depending on what I'm working on, and I think that's actually appropriate.

On the one hand, a big chunk of the technical safety work we do at DeepMind is pretty near-term in flavor. We're thinking about the models we have now and the ones we'll plausibly have in the next couple of years, and asking: how do we evaluate them for dangerous capabilities, how do we train them to be more honest and more aligned with what we actually want, how do we build the monitoring and oversight infrastructure so that if something starts going wrong, we notice. That work is grounded in concrete systems, which is nice, because you can actually run experiments and get feedback on whether your ideas are any good.

On the other hand, the reason I care about any of this is the longer horizon. The thing that motivates me is the possibility that we build systems that are broadly more capable than humans across most domains, and that we lose the ability to course-correct if they're pursuing goals we didn't intend. So I'm constantly trying to ask whether the near-term work is actually on a path toward solving that problem, or whether it's just making current systems a bit nicer in ways that won't scale.

I'd say I try to hold both frames at once. If you only think about the long term, you end up doing very abstract work that's hard to validate and that may be solving the wrong problem. If you only think about the next model, you risk optimising for things that look good today but don't address the fundamental issues. So the way I think about it is: we have a long-term goal, and we try to break that down into things we can make progress on now, while keeping a running check on whether the decomposition still makes sense as the technology changes. And honestly, the technology has changed fast enough that we revisit that decomposition more often than I would have predicted a few years ago.

astra-6.text:
I think the way I’d frame it is that we’re trying to anticipate the problems we’ll face as models become more capable, rather than planning around one particular date for AGI. You want a longer-term picture of what could go wrong and what a convincing approach to safety would look like. But then you need to work backwards from that to things you can actually investigate now.

There’s a balance there. If you only work on problems that show up in today’s systems, you might be unprepared for something that emerges quite quickly. If your work depends on a very detailed picture of what AGI will look like, there’s a good chance that picture will be wrong. So I’m interested in work that can teach us something today while still being relevant as capabilities increase.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different timescales. We’re thinking about what we can do now to make the next generation of models safer, but we’re also asking what we’ll need when we have systems that are substantially more capable than the ones we have today.

For the longer-term work, I find it more useful to think in terms of capabilities than calendar dates. If a system could carry out a long research project autonomously, for example, how would we know it was pursuing the goal we intended? What kinds of oversight would actually work? You can start investigating those questions now, even if current models aren’t yet capable enough to present the full problem.

So I wouldn’t describe it as having a detailed plan for a particular year. It’s more about anticipating what could change as capabilities improve, and trying to have the relevant safety techniques ready before we need them.
